nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:1}
	We say that the distribution $\mathbf P\!_n$ of data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n$ 
	is Gaussian with adversarial contamination, denoted by 
	$\mathbf P\!_n\in \textup{GAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$ with 
	$\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma\succeq 0$,
	if there is a set of $n$ independent and identically distributed random 
	vectors $\boldsymbol Y_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol Y_n$ drawn from $\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma)$ 
	satisfying
	\begin{align}
	\big|\{i:\boldsymbol X_i\neq \boldsymbol Y_i \}\big|\le \varepsilon n.
	\end{align}

nodes.raw_latex:
\small
				\STATE {\bfseries Input:} data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n\in\mathbb R^p$,  
				contamination rate $\varepsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma$
				\STATE {\bfseries Output:} parameter estimate $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$
				\STATE {\bfseries Initialize:} compute $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0$ as a minimizer of 
				$\sum_{i=1}^n \|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2$\\[7pt]
				\STATE  Set $K = 0\vee\Big\lceil \frac{\log(4\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}) - 2\log(\varepsilon({1-2\varepsilon}))}
				{2\log(1-2\varepsilon) - \log \varepsilon -\log(1-\varepsilon)}
				\Big\rceil$.\\[7pt]
				\STATE {{\bf For} $k=1:K$}
				
				
				
				
				\STATE \qquad {Compute current weights:}\\
				
				\qquad\quad $\displaystyle	\boldsymbol w \in \mathop{\textup{arg\,min}}_{(n-n\varepsilon)\|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le 1}
					\lambda_{\max}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n  w_i (\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})
					^{\otimes 2}- \boldsymbol\Sigma\bigg)\vee 0.		
				$
				
				\STATE \qquad{Update the estimator: $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\boldsymbol X_i$}.
				\STATE {\bfseries EndFor}
				\STATE {{\bf Return} $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}$}.

		that $|J|\ge \ell$, the uniform weight vector $\boldsymbol u^{J}\in 
		\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$.
		\item[\textup{  ii)}] The set $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ is 
		the convex hull of the uniform weight vectors $\{\boldsymbol u^{J} : 
		|J| = \ell\}$.

		$G:\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}\to\mathbb R$,  we have

		where the last maximum is over all subsets $J$ of cardinality 
		$\ell$ of the set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
		\item[\textup{ iv)}] If $\boldsymbol w\in\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ then for any 
		$I$ such that $|I|\ge \ell'>n-\ell$, we have 
		$\boldsymbol w_{|I}\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell+\ell'-n}$.
	\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: The proof of this theorem is deferred to the supplementary material. One can use Crefth:4 to construct an adaptive (with respect to varepsilon) estimator of boldsymbolmu^* in the case of unknown boldsymbolSigma using Lepski's method detailed in Crefssec:Lepski. For this construction, it suffices to know an upper bound sigma_max on the operator norm \|boldsymbolSigma\|^1/2_textupop. The resulting estimator has an error of the order sigma_max( sqrtp/n + sqrtvarepsilon). One can also consider intermediate cases, in which the covariance matrix is not arbitrary but has a more general form than the simple isotropic one. In such a situation, it might be of interest to extend the method proposed in Algorithm~ by using an initial estimator of boldsymbolSigma and by updating its value at each step. Indeed, when a weight vector is computed, it can be used for updating not only the mean but also the covariance matrix. The study of this estimator is left for future research.

nodes.statement: First, notice that it is sufficient to prove this bound for varepsilon > sqrttextupr_scriptscriptstyleboldsymbolSigma/n. Indeed, if varepsilon < sqrttextupr_scriptscriptstyleboldsymbolSigma/n then one gets the desired lower bound by simply comparing GAC model with the standard outlier free model. More formally, inf_widehatboldsymbolmu_n R_max(widehatboldsymbolmu_n, boldsymbolSigma, varepsilon) ge inf_widehatboldsymbolmu_n R_max^textupOF(widehatboldsymbolmu_n) = sqrtfracmathoptextupTrboldsymbolSigman, where R_max^textupOF(widehatboldsymbolmu_n) is the worst case risk in the classical outlier free setting where the observations are i.i.d. and drawn from N_p(boldsymbolmu^*, boldsymbolSigma). Since the GAC model is more general than HDC model, then one clearly has inf_widehatboldsymbolmu_n R_max(widehatboldsymbolmu_n, boldsymbolSigma, varepsilon) ge inf_widehatboldsymbolmu_n R_max^textupHDC(widehatboldsymbolmu_n, varepsilon). On the other hand, in view of Eq. (4) from citepbateni2020minimax, for every r>0, R_max^textupHDC(widehatboldsymbolmu_n, varepsilon) + r e^-nvarepsilon/6 ge sup_mathbf P_n in M^textupHC_n(0.5varepsilon, boldsymbolmu^*) rP big( \| widehatboldsymbolmu_n - boldsymbolmu \|_2 ge rbig). Using the result of Theorem and taking first r = C \| boldsymbolSigma\|_textupop^1/2big[sqrttextupr_scriptscriptstyleboldsymbolSigma/n + varepsilonbig] then infimum of both sides one arrives at inf_widehatboldsymbolmu_n R_max^textupHDC(widehatboldsymbolmu_n, varepsilon) ge (C/4) \| boldsymbolSigma\|_textupop^1/2bigg[sqrtfractextupr_scriptscriptstyleboldsymbolSigman + varepsilonbigg]big(1 - 2e^-nvarepsilon/6big). Now, using varepsilon > sqrttextupr_scriptscriptstyleboldsymbolSigma/n one gets that nvarepsilon > sqrttextupr_scriptscriptstyleboldsymbolSigma n ge sqrtn. Therefore, taking n ge 36log^2(4), one can check that yields inf_widehatboldsymbolmu_n R_max^textupHDC(widehatboldsymbolmu_n, 2varepsilon) ge (C/8) \| boldsymbolSigma\|_textupop^1/2bigg[sqrtfractextupr_scriptscriptstyleboldsymbolSigman + varepsilonbigg]. Then, the final result follows from with constants c = C/8 and widetildec = 36log^2(4).
